cover.title: The [[filesystem-service]]
cover.lead: One place where every NFS and SMB call is checked, in one order.
cover.notes: Source: docs/internals/rfcs/rfc-17-vfs.md, commit b0d540b. The RFC specifies behaviour, not the current code. Keys: → next, S speaker notes, ? help. Click any underlined term for its definition.

intro.two: The [[filesystem-service]] is the one interface every [[adapter]] calls, and it runs each operation's checks — on the share, the permission, the [[open-state|open state]] and the quota — always in the same order and in one place, for NFS and SMB alike. RFC 17 fixes that interface, which component owns what, the order of every call at the file's [[primary]], the node in charge of that file, and how a call reaches that primary in a cluster.
intro.twoNotes: From 'Start here · In plain words' and §1 Purpose. The RFC's own one-liner: the protocol layer translates, and one layer beneath it orders and enforces (Appendix A).
intro.knownLead: From RFC 0's glossary and the RFCs this one builds on (7, 8, 11, 14, 15, 16, 18, 20). Click one for its definition.
intro.knownNotes: Every definition is a plain restatement of RFC 0's glossary row, which is the definition of record.
intro.newNotes: From 'Start here · The words you need': filesystem / gateway, primary, open / anonymous open, admission, the chokepoint, caching grant, pseudo-filesystem. Plus the share grant (§4.6), retry-later (§4.3), WCC (§3.0), the lock order (§5.0), quota reservations (§5.6), delete on close (§5.3) and the route envelope (§2, RFC 15 §4.3).
intro.clashNotes: VFS: the package is named for the field's word for a protocol-neutral file API (§1), not for the Linux VFS, which Appendix A lists only as prior art. Filesystem: §2 uses it for *vfs.Filesystem. Grant: the share grant (§4.6), the open-time grant (§4.6, RFC 7 §7.2) and the caching grant (§3.2) are three things. Release: RFC 0's glossary gives it two senses; RFC 17 §5.3 uses the file sense. Handle and lease: RFC 0.

problem.title: Two protocols, one file, no shared rule
problem.lead: alice-pc keeps `profiles/alice/ODFC_alice.vhdx` open over SMB all day, with a deny mode that forbids anyone else to write to it. A script on build01 writes to the same file over NFSv3, a protocol with no notion of opening a file.
problem.smb: If each adapter put a call's checks together on its own, the SMB adapter would check alice's [[deny-mode]], because deny modes are part of SMB.
problem.nfsTitle: An NFSv3 adapter on its own
problem.nfs: The NFSv3 adapter, written for a protocol without opens, would not check it. build01's write would go straight into the [[journal]], in the middle of a virtual disk that Windows has mounted.
problem.outcome: The disk is corrupt, and no log anywhere shows a conflict.
problem.notes: 'Start here · The problem, with one example'. This is the RFC's own scenario and the running example of this deck: alice-pc over SMB, build01 over NFSv3.

sixsteps.title: With the service: one rule, one place
sixsteps.notes: 'Start here', steps 1–3 and its figure (img/rfc17-six-steps.svg): route (the gateway's, in a cluster only), then in the filesystem admit, authorise, check open state, reserve quota, engine. alice-pc passes through her own open; the engine stages the bytes in the journal. The picture's numbering is the 'Start here' figure's; §5.1's write table numbers its steps differently (there the deny-mode check for an anonymous open is step 2). Which NFS status the adapter answers is RFC 21 §11.5's.

promises.title: What RFC 17 promises
items: Every call that names a [[handle]] or an open is admitted to its [[share]], whatever path the handle came by. A client removed from a share is refused on its very next call, even if it still holds handles.
A conflict between two protocols is decided in one place. The check and the I/O it allows run as one step at the file's [[primary]], so nothing can be granted in between.
No server worker sits waiting for a client to answer.
promises.analogy: A hotel whose guests speak two languages. Interpreters at the door translate, and one reception desk checks every request against the same rules. Where the analogy stops holding: in a cluster each file has its own desk, at its [[primary]], and every door sends the guest to that desk.
promises.notes: 'Start here · What this RFC promises' and 'In plain words' (the hotel is the RFC's own analogy; its limit is the deck's, from §2 and §4.8). The quota promise in full: writers spread over several primaries overshoot a hard limit by a stated bound at most (§5.6). Admission covers every call that names a handle or an open; sign-in and principal spellings act on no share and are not admitted (§3.1, Principals; V12).
more: Adapters never see the cluster. A call the gateway forwarded, and resent because its reply was lost, is applied only once.
Quota is enforced here and nowhere else.
promises.moreNotes: Same source as the previous slide: 'Start here · What this RFC promises'. A forwarded call resent after a lost reply is answered once by Serve's dedup table (RFC 15 §4.3, the route envelope). Quota: §5.6; writers spread over several primaries overshoot a hard limit by a stated bound at most.

impls.title: One interface, two implementations
table: decides everything about a call, at the file's [[primary]]: [[admission]], the caller's identity, the order of every step, [[open-state|open state]], metadata and content
what the adapters are handed in a cluster. It sends each call to the file's primary, re-routes a call that reached the wrong node, and resends a call whose reply was lost
decides or admits a call, or answers one itself, except with `ErrUnavailable` while it stops or when no primary answers in time

checks every call that reaches a primary. It refuses a call carrying an out-of-date [[node-epoch|node epoch]] or [[epoch|shard epoch]], numbers that rise when a node restarts or a new primary takes over. It answers a resent call from its [[dedup-table|dedup table]], and otherwise calls the filesystem
forwards a call to another node
impls.footer: On a single node the [[adapter|adapters]] are handed the filesystem itself, and in a cluster they are handed the gateway. An adapter cannot tell which of the two it holds. Only the filesystem calls the metadata store, the [[engine]], open state and identity, the component that signs callers in and maps them to users.
impls.notes: §2's table and deployment table; §2.3 for the wiring. Decision in §2: the cut between nodes is vfs.Service, not the service–engine interface, so open state lives beside the I/O it gates, a WRITE is one forwarded call carrying its bytes, and one shard epoch fences the whole call. Decision in §2.1: one component calls the store and the engine, so a transaction boundary, a retry, a fence and a cache key are each decided once. Serve fences each call on the sender's node epoch, the shard epoch and a hop count of zero (§2's table); a shard epoch rises when a new primary takes over (RFC 11, RFC 15 §4.3). Identity is RFC 18's: SignIn delegates to its authenticator, and the resolver maps an Identity to a caller on a share (§2, §4.9 step 4).

route.title: The [[gateway-node|gateway]] routes, the [[primary]] decides
route.notes: (cluster) §2, §2.1, §4.7, RFC 15 §4.3. A call naming a handle goes to the primary of that handle's shard; Rename and Link to RFC 15 §4.2's coordinator; Copy and Clone to the destination's primary; calls naming no file run on the local filesystem and are never forwarded. A handle the router cannot place goes to the local filesystem, which admits before answering ErrStale. An adapter names each call's request ID with vfs.WithRequestID; repeating a mutation is not assumed safe. Serve fences each call on the node epoch, the shard epoch and a hop count of zero, and the checked Service it returns runs the same checks on the gateway's local path (§2's table).

owners.title: Who owns [[open-state|open state]] and locks
table: the protocol side of a [[lock-waiter|waiting lock]], a lock request that waits for its range to be free: the request it answers and the [[nlm|NLM]] host it calls back
holds any open state, since it routes every lock and open call to the file's primary
filesystem on the node the client is connected to, its [[lease-owner|lease owner]], which may not be the file's primary
each client's [[client-lease|lease]] record and the [[callback]] channel that reaches the client
owners.footer: The open-state table lives in memory and is keyed by file. When another node [[takeover|takes over]] as primary, the table is lost, and clients rebuild it by reclaiming their state during the [[grace-period|grace period]], for that [[shard]] alone. In exchange, a lock costs one hop to the primary and no write to the store.
owners.notes: §2.2. Decisions there: open state is its own component, neither in the store (every lock would be a store transaction) nor in the engine (unlink, rename and delete on close never call the engine); and there is no separate distributed lock manager, which would add a hop and a window to every write. Locking scales across shards, not within one hot shard. §2.1: a call that names no file runs on the local filesystem, which is the lease owner of the clients connected to its node, while a file's calls go to its shard's primary.
table2: the open-state table: opens, [[deny-mode|deny modes]], byte-range locks from NLM, NFSv4 and SMB alike, [[caching-grant|caching grants]] and [[watch|watches]]
only what is kept across a restart: client records, persistent SMB opens, and the durable open records that keep an unlinked file alive
owners.notes2: §2.2: the filesystem at the file's primary holds RFC 14's open-state table and runs the conflict check and the I/O it admits under the file's accept lock, with nothing between (§4.8, V7). The table is lost at failover and rebuilt by grace reclaims for that shard alone (RFC 14 §4.2).

areas.title: Seven areas, one `vfs.Service`
areas.union: The set is the **union** of what the protocols need, not the intersection. `Open` takes disposition, access, [[deny-mode]] and [[caching-grant]] in one atomic step, because SMB needs them together, and NFSv3 reads and writes run on an [[anonymous-open]]. An [[adapter]] never imitates a protocol by combining weaker calls.
areas.notes: §3.1 (decision: one interface per area, embedded, and no finer — NLM needs Locking and Clients, rquota Shares) and §4.1. If SMB's atomic create-with-deny were built from a lookup, a create and an open, two clients could interleave between them: the service offers the atomic form, or the operation is not supported. MoveTarget names another gateway node serving the share while this node drains, for an adapter's ErrMoved and NFSv4's fs_locations; with no such node it answers none, as on a single node (§3.1, §4.9).

wcc.title: Every change answers with its own attributes
wcc.ret: Each call that changes something returns the attributes of every object it changed, before and after the change, both read during a single hold of the file's lock. No handler follows a change with a `GetAttr`, which could show another client's write as if it were this one's. `Copy` and `Clone` are the exception: their after-attributes are read once the engine answers, with no lock held across the clone.
wcc.read: `Lookup`, `ReadDir`, `GetAttr`, `Read`, `Seek`, `TestLock`, `Root` and a few more change nothing, so one request may make any number of them. Every other method may change state, and a handler makes at most one such call per request, apart from session setup.
wcc.version: `GetAttr` combines the metadata store's record with the writes the [[engine]] has staged but the store has not yet recorded. So a file's `Version`, a number that rises with each change to the file, goes up with every write the primary accepts, not only when the store records it, and it never moves backward.
wcc.notes: §3.1 ('Every mutating call returns the attributes', 'Which calls change state', vfs.Mutates), §5.7 (GetAttr and the overlay; Before is nil where the lock cannot be taken, and never for a directory over NFSv3), V16, V31. The engine's overlay is the Size, Times and Version of the operations staged but not yet committed (§5.7). Session setup (SMB SESSION_SETUP, NFSv4.1 CREATE_SESSION) makes the Principals calls and its client-record calls outside the one-call rule, as RFC 20 §4.3 lists (§3.1). MoveTarget is among the calls that change nothing (§3.1). Copy and Clone: their Before is read under the destination's accept lock in the admitted hook, their After once the engine answers, with no lock held across the clone (§5.9 step 4, V31).

notyours.title: State belongs to whoever it was granted to
items: Every [[open-state|open state]] call names the client making it. An open, a [[caching-grant]], a [[watch]] or a [[lock-owner|lock owner]] that this client does not hold is refused with [[not-yours|NotYours]].
Naming the right client is not enough. One client can carry the calls of several users, and the access an open was granted serves only the [[principal]], the user, it was granted to.
If bob presents alice's open to write, he is refused with `NotYours`, even on a file bob may write himself, and alice's open stays intact.

A [[delegation]] belongs to the client, not to one opener. I/O under it is allowed only if the calling client holds it on a [[session]], is checked against the caller's own principal, and gains no access from the delegation.
notyours.footer: A call made outside any [[session]] that presents state created on a session is refused with `NotYours` too. NFSv4.0 has no sessions, so it is never offered a delegation.
notyours.notes: §3.1, 'Every open-state call names the client', 'Naming the right client is not enough' and 'A delegation is the client's'; V8, V18, V24. Under NFSv4.0 a stateid names the client only through the state, so anyone who learns it could present it — hence the principal check. The refused IDs are OpenID, GrantID, WatchID and lock owner (§3.1). A client may act for several principals: an NFSv4 client may do I/O under its delegation for any of its open-owners and principals (§3.1, RFC 8881 §9.1.3).

recall.title: [[callback|Callbacks]]: no worker waits on a client
recall.notes: §3.2 and its figure (img/rfc17-recall.svg). The NFS adapter answers the protocol's retry signal: NFS4ERR_DELAY, or NFS3ERR_JUKEBOX over NFSv3. If the conflicting caller is an SMB client, the SMB adapter sends an interim response and re-drives the call itself, held up to recall_timeout, which exceeds the break deadline (RFC 20 §4.6, RFC 22 §16.5). The 35 s break deadline is RFC 14 §5.3's, for SMB.

recallrules.title: When a client does not answer
items: A [[callback]] never blocks the service past its deadline. A callback that fails or times out counts as the client not answering.
If a client does not acknowledge a recall by its deadline, the grant is revoked, and that client is offered no new grants for one [[client-lease|client lease]] period, 90 s.

When an SMB break times out, the lease is forced down to no caching. The conflicting request, which the SMB adapter [[held-request|held]] meanwhile, proceeds. The client's opens stay, with their locks and [[deny-mode|deny modes]].
Once an NFS delegation is revoked, later writes under it are refused.
An SMB break is sent to a session that holds one of the [[lease|lease's]] opens, or that is signed in as one of its openers. It is never addressed by a `ClientGuid`, which any client could send.
recallrules.footer: The service waits inside a call in one case only. A call that meets a [[clone]] or a copy still running on the same bytes waits for it, but only as long as the adapter allows.
recallrules.notes: §3.2: the MUSTs on callbacks, 'Recalls after one is revoked', 'An SMB break goes by its open', V6, V36. A request held behind a recall MUST be held past the break deadline (35 s for SMB), and one held behind a freeze past migration.freeze_timeout plus the break deadline; RFC 13 refuses settings that break either. ErrBlocked holds no worker and has no deadline. The one wait inside a call: behind a running clone or a copy's chunk, bounded by the adapter's WithHold (§5.9). 'One lease period' is the client lease, 90 s (RFC 14). SMB cannot tell a client to retry, so its adapter holds the request and re-drives it (§3.2, RFC 20 §4.6).

errors.title: Errors are neutral values
table: The [[share-grant|share grant]], the share's client rules, or the file's mode or ACL refuse the caller.
Refused whatever access the caller has: the file is immutable or append-only, or only its owner may make the change.
The [[handle]] names nothing, or names a share being removed or already retired.
A [[deny-mode]] held by another open conflicts. If that open lives on only through an SMB client's [[handle-caching|handle caching]], the service first breaks the caching and decides on the retry.
Another owner holds a conflicting byte-range lock. The error names that lock owner, never its principal.
errors.footer: Every error is declared once, in `pkg/vfs/vfserr`. `vfs.Errors()` lists them all, so a test can check that each adapter's error table covers every one.
errors.notes: §4.3: a selection of the table, which also has ErrNotFound, ErrExist, ErrNotEmpty, ErrNotDir, ErrIsDir, ErrReadOnly, ErrNameTooLong, ErrInvalid, ErrRangeNotLocked, ErrDeletePending, ErrBlocked, ErrWrongSecurity, ErrCross, ErrIncomplete, ErrInconsistent, ErrLost, ErrUnavailable, ErrCorrupt, ErrIO and ErrPastEnd. vfserr is a leaf importing only the standard library, so the engine can return ErrDelay and ErrCross without importing pkg/vfs. ErrFileOpen is the one value not re-exported: only the service reads it. ErrShareViolation comes after the handle-caching grants covering the conflicting opens are broken (§4.6 'Deny modes', §5.3).
table2: The [[shard]] is in its grace period, and the call needs, or conflicts with, state that may still be reclaimed.
A [[retry-later]] refusal: the client tries again shortly, and the error always says why.
`ErrNoSpace` is a permanent refusal for lack of capacity, `ErrQuota` a refusal by a logical quota. Both are answered at once.

A name for state that the client presents cannot be used: [[not-yours|NotYours]] (it is another client's or user's), `StaleState` (it may have been lost with its shard's open state) or `BadState` (no such state exists).
errors.notes2: §4.3, continued: the rest of the selection. ErrQuota carries the scope that was exceeded, first of share, project, user and group. StateError's kinds (NotYours, StaleState, BadState and the others) and the DelayCause values are listed in §4.3. StaleState: a stateid or FileId whose state may have been lost with its shard's open state; BadState: every other one whose record is missing — expired, freed, never issued (§4.3). ErrGrace carries *Grace{Until}, when the shard's grace ends, so a holding adapter bounds its hold from the error (§4.3, RFC 20 §4.6). StateError also has NoGrace, a reclaim from a client with nothing left to reclaim (§4.3).

delay.title: [[retry-later|ErrDelay]] always says why
causes: `DelayClone` — a [[clone]] or copy still running holds the bytes the call touches
`DelayConflict` — two changes to the same metadata collided, and the store's retries had not settled it by the deadline
`DelayFrozen` — an administrator has paused (quiesced) the share, or it is frozen for a [[namespace-move|move]], or it has moved away
`DelayCapacity` — the [[journal]] is full, or the share has used up its own limit in it
`DelayResources` — one of the node's memory pools is used up
`DelayJournal` — the local [[journal]] is read-only for now: a device error that may clear, or a share removal waiting for the journal to reopen
rules: A temporary refusal never turns into `ErrNoSpace` just because a deadline ran out.
A conflict still present at the deadline is answered `DelayConflict`, never an I/O error.
A routing refusal never reaches an [[adapter]], because the gateway re-routes the call itself.
An NFS adapter passes the retry on to its client, while an SMB adapter [[held-request|holds the request]]. How long depends on the cause, never on the operation.
delay.notes: §4.3, the Delay type and the paragraph after it; §3.2 ('How long a delayed request may be held'). Every call carries the pipeline's per-attempt deadline (RFC 20 §6.4); the service sets none. Causes are abbreviated here: DelayFrozen also covers a share not attached here, a shard not yet served, and content not yet reconciled after damage; DelayCommit also covers quota slack spent (cluster) and a stable write's sync that may have lost it. Quiesced is a share state the management API sets and clears (RFC 16 §2.3.1). A metadata conflict is a write-write conflict the store detects optimistically and retries until the deadline (RFC 0 §9.2). DelayJournal: the local journal is read-only for now, after a device error that may clear, or for a removal past its journal step waiting for the reopen (§4.3, RFC 8 §8.1, §11.2). Zero is no cause: every Delay names one of the eight (§4.3).

chokepoint.title: One [[chokepoint]] decides permissions
chokepoint.order: Every call: **[[admission]]** → **authorisation** → **conflict check**, in that order.
items: Only the chokepoint in the metadata store decides permissions, and the service's `authz` package is the only code that calls it.

The [[share-grant]] is read at admission on every call, and the chokepoint applies it as a ceiling on what the file allows. A cached decision has the grant list's version in its key, so a changed or deleted grant is never answered from the cache.
A call made through an open is decided by the access stored with that open. An anonymous call, or one with no open, checks the caller afresh.
An open is decided together with its parent directory. So SMB's `DELETE` access comes from the right to delete a child of that directory, as an NFS remove does.
Holding a [[handle]] grants nothing: every call on it is authorised afresh.
chokepoint.notes: §4.6 and its code sketch; RFC 7 §7.1, §7.5, §7.7. A cache of authorisation results MUST include the share's grant-list version and the parent directory with its whole record's version in its key. A privileged grant (backup intent) makes every request through that open privileged (V-row §4.6). The chokepoint emits no event; the filesystem builds every access event (§3.3).

admission.title: [[admission|Admission]]: five checks on every call to a share
steps: **Share state.** A share an administrator has paused answers `ErrDelay`, and one being removed or retired answers `ErrStale`.
**Security minimums.** How the call was proved and protected is compared with the share's minimums, and a call below them gets `ErrWrongSecurity`.
**Client rules.** The client's address and netgroups may refuse the call with `ErrAccess`, or limit it to read-only.

**Resolution.** The service maps the caller's [[identity]], applies squashing, collects the user's groups and reads the [[share-grant|share grant]]. This step refuses nothing. The chokepoint applies the grant afterwards.
**Share cap.** If the share is already using its limit of the node's request buffers, the call gets `ErrDelay` at once.
admission.footer: Admission runs before the [[handle]] is resolved, so a refused client learns nothing about the file. No call to a share skips it: not a lock, an unlock or a watch, not an NFSv4 `PUTFH`, nor a walk down from the [[pseudo-filesystem]].
admission.notes: §4.9 and its figure. Step 5 does not apply to a call that only releases state (close, unlock, cancel, a grant return, freeing a state ID) or reclaims it; steps 1, 2 and 4 still gate those, and step 3's refusal does not apply to a call that only releases state. A compound crossing into another share is re-admitted and re-resolved at the crossing. Steps 1–4 may be cached per (share, identity) only with the policy, netgroup, share-list and grant-list versions and the principals generation in the key, plus the client address when a client rule decided; step 5 is never cached. V12, V39. A paused share is in the quiesced state (§4.9 step 1, RFC 16 §2.3.1). Resolution refuses nothing; Authorize applies the share access it read as the share ceiling (§4.6). Sign-in and principal spellings act on no share and are not admitted (§3.1, Principals).

revoked.title: bob loses his [[share-grant]]
revoked.lead: An administrator removes bob's grant on `profiles` while bob-pc still holds [[handle|handles]].
steps: bob-pc's next call presents a handle it got earlier.
[[admission|Admission]] runs, as on every call, and reads bob's share grant afresh. It finds none, but admission does not refuse on that. It passes bob's share access, now none, on to the next check.
The [[chokepoint]] applies that share access as a ceiling on what the file allows. With no grant left, it refuses the call with `ErrAccess`. Holding a handle grants nothing.
Any cache of permission results has the grant in its key, so no stale "yes" survives.
revoked.outcome: Losing access takes effect on the next call, not at the next mount.
revoked.notes: 'Start here · Scenarios', the RFC's own scenario; §4.6; V9. Admission's resolution step reads the caller's share access from the grants and refuses nothing (§4.9 step 4); Authorize applies that access as the share ceiling (§4.6, 'The share grant is checked on every call'), and a refused share grant is ErrAccess (§4.3).

reaching.title: Reaching a [[share]], and removing one
root: An NFSv3 `MNT`, an NFSv4 `PUTROOTFH` and an SMB `TREE_CONNECT` each become one `Root` call.
That call is where a client fails early, but it is not where access is gated: every later call is admitted again.
The [[pseudo-filesystem]] is built from the share list, the same on every node.
Nothing is stored for a mount, a tree connect or a session, and the NFSv3 MOUNT table is not kept either.
reaching.removeTitle: A removal waits for admitted calls
remove: [[admission|Admission]] counts each call against its share **before** reading the share's state.
To remove a share, the control plane only marks it. The node then waits with `JoinShare` until no admitted call remains, and `DropShare` ends the share's [[open-state|open state]].
A call counted after the mark sees it and is refused with `ErrStale`.
The adapters are told what the share held through a `RevokedShare` notice, so they can answer the requests they still hold on it.
reaching.notes: §4.9 ('The service owns every step of reaching a share', 'Neither is stored', the MOUNT-table decision, 'A share's removal joins the calls admitted before it'), §3.2 ('A share removed or moved'), §2.5, V13, V40. Decision: share resolution and the pseudo-filesystem live in the service because the rules drifted when each adapter had its own copy. §2.5: the control plane's DeleteShare only marks the share and returns; the node calls JoinShare, §4.9's join, then RFC 14's DropShare, and a crash between the mark and the join leaves a marked share the next start finishes.

lockorder.title: One [[lock-order|lock order]] for every call
levels: First, the [[admission-lock|admission lock]] of every file the call touches. The call holds it across a check on [[open-state|open state]] and the change or I/O that check allows.

Then [[fold-admission|fold admission]] at every directory the call changes. A change adds a small update to the directory's counts and times instead of rewriting them, and a [[delta-fold|fold]] later merges the updates. Fold admission makes new changes wait while a fold runs. A call that cannot pass every gate by its deadline answers `ErrDelay`.
Last, the [[accept-lock|accept lock]] of every file the call changes. The call holds it while the change takes its version number and is applied, so the attributes read before and after are exact.
lockorder.heldTitle: A call that waits holds no lock
lockorder.held: The service makes a write wait while a [[clone]] is still copying the bytes the write touches. During that wait the write gives up its locks and its [[quota-reservation|quota reservation]], and it runs its checks again when the wait ends.
lockorder.notes: §5.0, 'One lock order, for every call'. The admission lock is the open-state step's outer level, under which a call makes every check on a file and the change it admits (§4.8). Fold admission covers every directory whose deltas the call writes, or whose own attributes it changes (§5.0; RFC 7 §9.2, §9.4). The accept lock is held while a change draws its version and is applied (§5.1 step 6, §5.7). Each level is taken in file-ID order. A call queued for fold admission holds no accept lock, and one waiting for an accept lock already holds every open-state step it needs, so a write and an unlink of the file's last name never each hold what the other waits for. The table's own entry mutex is a leaf, never held when a call returns. V29 races these 10⁴ times.
lockorder.order: Within each level, a call takes its locks in the order of the files' IDs. Because every call takes them in the same order, no two calls can each hold what the other is waiting for.
lockorder.heldWhy: If the waiting write kept its locks, every open, close and lock on the file would wait as well, and so would the client's acknowledgement of a [[lease]] break. The break could then run out, and the lease would be revoked.
lockorder.heldNotes: §5.0, 'A held call holds nothing': a call held behind a clone or a copy's chunk (§5.9) releases its accept lock, every open-state step it took and its quota reservation for the length of the hold, and re-runs §5.1's steps 3–6 when the hold ends. Holding them, every open, close, lock and break acknowledgement on the file would wait with it, long enough for a lease break to run out and be revoked. V29 tests it with a 1 GiB clone under writes and a pending lease break.

write.title: A write, step by step
table: [[admission|Admit]] the call to the share, counting it first, and resolve the [[handle]].
Through an open, check that the caller is the open's principal, then use the open's grant. On an anonymous open, check the caller afresh, then the [[deny-mode|deny modes]] that others hold.

During a [[grace-period|grace period]], refuse with `ErrGrace` a write that meets state a client may still reclaim. Then check byte-range locks. A conflicting [[caching-grant]] starts a recall, and the call answers `ErrDelay`.
[[quota-reservation|Reserve quota]] for what the write adds: the holes it fills plus the bytes past the end of the file.
write.footer: Steps 3 to 6 run at the [[primary]] as one step. The [[accept-lock|accept lock]] is never held across a sync, or across a [[group-commit|group commit]], the one metadata transaction that records many writes at once.
write.notes: §5.1's table and code sketch. Step 2 for an anonymous or delegated write asks write data below the size, and at or past it write data where the caller holds it, append data otherwise. Step 6: any change refused ErrVersionBehind is redrawn and retried within the deadline, never surfaced. V3 tests each order by what a refusal leaves unchanged: a write refused at step 3 holds no reservation, stages no byte and clears no setuid bit. Each order runs in the filesystem at the file's primary, where the gateway has routed the call (§5's introduction), so routing is not a step here. Step 3's grace check: RFC 14 §4.4. 'The lock never spans a sync or a group commit' (§5.1) is step 6's accept lock. Stable writes: §5.1, 'Which writes are stable'. A write of no byte runs steps 1–3 only, crossing no lock and starting no recall, and returns the file's WCC unchanged: it reserves nothing, clears no setuid bit and changes no time (§5.1, V22).
table2: Refuse with `ErrPerm` an immutable file, or an append-only one written below its end. For an unprivileged caller, clear setuid and setgid in a committed change.
Under the [[accept-lock|accept lock]], capture the [[wcc|WCC]] before, call the [[engine]]'s `Write`, and capture the WCC after.
Reply. A stable write, one that survives a crash once acknowledged, first waits for the [[journal]] to sync it.
write.lead: The table starts at the [[primary]], after the gateway's routing, and groups the checks differently from the six-step picture, so its numbers do not match the picture's.
write.title2: A write, step by step, continued
write.notes2: §5.1's table, steps 5 to 7, and the sentence after it: 'Steps 3–6 run at the primary as one step (§4.8), except across a hold (§5.0). The lock never spans a sync or a group commit.' The lock is step 6's accept lock. Stable writes: §5.1, 'Which writes are stable'.

stable.title: When a write is stable
write: A write is stable when the client asks for it. It is always stable through a [[persistent-open|persistent open]] or on a [[continuously-available|continuously available]] share, because those opens survive a restart, and so do the writes they acknowledged.
A stable write is answered only after the [[journal]] has [[sync|synced]] it to the local disk.

If the write overwrites bytes whose [[existence]] the metadata store has already recorded, it also waits for the [[existence|existence commit]]. After a crash, the synced journal alone can rebuild an append or a hole fill, but an overwrite also needs its record in metadata.
When the journal is full, a write gets `ErrDelay` (`DelayCapacity`) for as long as [[offload]] or [[repack]] can still free space, never `ErrNoSpace`.
read: A read returns only bytes that have been verified, streamed by the [[engine]].

It may return `n` good bytes and then an error for the bytes after them, for example because they are [[lost|Lost]]. The adapter answers a short read of the `n` bytes when `n > 0` and its protocol allows it.
Bytes that failed are never replaced with zeros.
Where a file's holes and data lie is answered by the [[engine]] too, so no [[adapter]] works it out by reading the file.
stable.notes: §5.1 ('Which writes are stable', step 7, the capacity paragraph); V19, V20. Stable when asked: NFS FILE_SYNC or DATA_SYNC, SMB write-through. Committed content is content whose existence the metadata store has recorded (RFC 8 §5.1): a stable append past the committed size, or a fill of a committed hole, waits only for the sync, and one whose extent covers committed content also waits for a recorded sync mark. A durable open that is not persistent is not reclaimable across a restart of the primary, so its writes need not be stable. A logical quota refuses at once (§5.6). Why: appends and hole fills are recoverable from synced records, which recovery re-applies; an overwrite of committed content is recorded by its existence commit's overwrite record (RFC 8 §5.1, RFC 6 §3.3).
stable.smb: SMB has no verifier. An SMB `FLUSH` that spans such a loss fails instead with `ErrLost`, which says that acknowledged data was lost, once for each open of the file.
stable.verifierNotes: §5.8. Write returns the verifier sampled before the bytes are staged, and Commit the one sampled once its sync has completed, so a loss before or during that sync makes them differ. The verifier is the engine's (RFC 8 §4.1), which folds in the journal's loss generation. A stable write answers the verifier its Write returned, never its Commit's, and ErrDelay (DelayCommit) when they differ, since a client does not consult the verifier of a stable reply. SMB: open state's Flushed fails the flush with ErrLost once for each open that was open across a loss of an acknowledged, unoffloaded write (RFC 14 §8.1). V25, V42. The verifier's inputs are the primary's node and node epoch, a process instance ID, the shard's incarnation and the journal's loss generation (RFC 8 §4.1); the loss generation rises only on loss events. A changed verifier makes the client resend its unstable writes (RFC 8 §4.1).
stable.readNotes: §5.2. The engine's Read resolves residency and streams verified chunks (RFC 8 §7.2); it can return n verified bytes and then ErrLost, ErrUnavailable, ErrCorrupt or ErrIO for the chunk after them. ErrUnavailable is transient and held (§3.2). SEEK_DATA, SEEK_HOLE, READ_PLUS's allocated ranges and SMB's allocated-range query come from the engine's Allocation (RFC 8 §7.6); no adapter derives them from reads. Seek from at or past the end is ErrPastEnd; it takes no byte-range lock and recalls no grant, so it can miss bytes another client caches under a write grant.
verifierItems: The verifier is built from several numbers. Two of them are the [[node-epoch|node epoch]], which rises when the node restarts, and the journal's [[loss-generation|loss generation]], which rises at each [[loss-event|loss]].
`Write` samples the verifier before it stages the bytes, and `Commit` samples it again after the sync. If the two differ, a loss may have taken the write in between.

After unstable writes, a changed verifier tells the client to send them again. A client does not check the verifier of a stable reply, so such a stable write is answered `ErrDelay` instead of success, and the client sends it again.

open.title: Open, close, and the sharing violation
open.lead: `Open` resolves or creates the name, checks the caller's permission and the [[deny-mode|deny modes]], offers a [[caching-grant]] and records the open. The protocol sees all of this as one step, run at the file's [[primary]].
open.violation: An SMB [[lease]] with handle caching keeps handles open that its client has already closed. A request that conflicts with the deny modes of such opens is not refused yet. The service breaks the lease first, answers `ErrDelay`, and checks again when the request is retried.
open.undo: If something fails after [[open-state|open state]] has recorded the open, for example the truncate an overwrite asks for, the service undoes the open with `Opens.Abandon`. If that leaves a file with no name and no open, the file is released, as at a last close.
open.notes: §5.3. The sharing-violation rule applies whatever the protocol: an SMB or NFSv4 open, an anonymous NFSv3 read or write, I/O under a delegation, an NFS REMOVE or RENAME against a deny-delete. Refused at once, it fails against handles nobody is using. V21.

release.title: [[delete-pending|Delete on close]], and releases
doc: Delete on close is a mark in [[open-state|open state]]. The file keeps its name until its last open closes.
Then `Close` runs a deferred unlink, as the principal who marked the file and with the access of the open that set the mark.
A directory marked this way takes no new entries, over any protocol.
If the unlink is still refused at that point, the refusal is logged and counted, and the file keeps its name.
moments: When an unlink or a rename leaves a file with no name and no open.
At the last close of a file with no name, whether the client closes it or the open-state table closes it itself.
After a file's release commits, for each of its [[named-stream|named streams]], which that release recorded as still to be released.

After a restart, for every [[pending-release|pending release]], once its shard's [[grace-period]] ends. An unlink records a pending release in its own transaction, so a crash before the release leaks nothing.
release.notes: §5.3 ('Delete on close is a mark and a deferred unlink', 'The service runs every release'), §5.4, V17, V28, V38. The deferred unlink takes the parent's step only after releasing the file's, to avoid deadlocking with an unlink of another of the file's names. A crash between the unlink and the release leaks nothing: the pending-release record is written in the unlink's transaction. An unlink whose name is gone succeeds whatever the engine's Delete answers. Named streams: the file's release writes their pending releases, and each is run when that release commits (§5.3, RFC 7 §4.3). Recovery runs every pending release when the table raises GraceEnded for the shard (§2.5, §5.3).

quota.title: [[quota|Quota]]: hard, soft and advisory limits
items: A write sets aside a [[quota-reservation|reservation]] for what it adds before anything changes. The [[existence|existence commit]] that records the write releases it, or the call's failure does.
One [[primary]] sees every reservation, so a hard limit is passed by at most what commits running at the same moment add.

In a cluster, a primary sees only its own reservations. So each primary may hold at most a fixed amount uncommitted, its slack, and writers through `k` primaries can pass a hard limit by at most `(k − 1)` × slack more.
A create charges the new file's owner, never the parent directory's owner. A privileged caller is held to the limit too.
quota.footer: The slack is the smaller of a set size and a set fraction of the hard limit, both chosen by the operator in the configuration.
quota.notes: §5.6, 'Soft limits', and Reserve's scopes. Scopes are checked in the order share, project, user, group; QuotaError names the first exceeded. The metadata store records when the soft limit was first exceeded; once the grace time has run from then, the soft limit is enforced as the hard one, and falling back under it clears the record. Each crossing emits a quota event (§3.3). 'Quota is not a permission' (§5.5).
model: A [[quota]] limits the bytes and files that a share, a project, a user or a group may use. Each has a hard limit, and may have a soft limit and an advisory threshold.
A write that would pass the hard limit is refused at once with `ErrQuota`.
Passing the soft limit refuses nothing at first. Once the soft limit's grace time has run out, the soft limit is enforced like the hard one.
Crossing the advisory threshold, or the soft limit, emits an event and refuses nothing.
Only the service refuses for quota. Neither the metadata store nor the [[engine]] does.
quota.notes2: §5.6 and §5.5 (owner and group changes move the charge); V10, V37. The group commit records existence and usage and releases the reservation (§5.1 step 7). A reservation is volatile: after a crash the journal re-applies the writes and their charge. Overshoot bound and (cluster) slack: §5.6. The slack is min(S, f × Hard), where S and f are RFC 13 settings and the derivation is RFC 16 §4.4's; a primary past its slack answers ErrDelay (DelayCommit). Ponytail: no slack while every primary of a share is one node.

copy.title: Copy and clone
copy.clone: A [[clone]] covers one [[extent]] and is answered only when it is done. A clone longer than the configured maximum is refused as invalid (`ErrInvalid`), all or nothing. In a cluster, a clone between files of two [[shard|shards]] is refused (`ErrCross`) and changes nothing, so the client copies the bytes itself.
copy.copy: A copy runs in bounded chunks, each one a small atomic clone. At its deadline it answers the bytes of the chunks already done and starts no other. The chunk under way still completes, and the client continues from the count, rewriting that chunk. A copy is always synchronous. In a cluster, the service itself copies the bytes between shards.
copy.hold: A write into an extent that a running clone copies from or to waits until the clone ends, but only as long as the [[adapter]] allows for that call. After that, it gets `ErrDelay` (`DelayClone`). A source range that is [[lost|Lost]] is copied as Lost, never as zeros.
copy.notes: §5.9, V26, V30. Also refused before anything changes: overlapping extents within one file (ErrInvalid), a copy across namespaces (ErrCross, CrossNamespace), an Incomplete source (ErrIncomplete). RFC 14's asynchronous copy state is unused until a client is shown to need offload. Without WithHold the answer is ErrDelay at once, which would cost an NFSv3 client its retry pause of several seconds. The configured maximum is clone_max_len (RFC 13); the adapter bounds the wait per call with WithHold (§5.9). Also refused before anything changes: a copy or clone whose range ends past the source's size (ErrInvalid, RFC 7862 §15.2.3); a source truncated once the copy has begun ends it with a short count. At the deadline the chunk under way completes past the count, since a chunk past its journal step can be neither undone nor waited for; the client's continuing copy is a clone into that chunk's destination, held until the chunk ends, so its bytes are the ones left (§5.9, V26). The admitted hook clears setuid and setgid on the destination once the engine has registered the clone (§5.9 step 4).

locks.title: Locks
items: A lock request takes all its ranges in one step, all or none, and only a request for a single range may wait.
A waiting lock (`ErrBlocked`) holds no worker and has no deadline. `LockWaitOver` tells the client later when it is granted.
When an NLM host does not answer a grant, the grant is sent again. A lock is never released because a host stayed silent.
A lock under no open, as NLM takes, needs read access to the file's data or ownership of the file, for a shared and an exclusive lock alike.
Through an open, checking that the caller is the opener is the whole check. Unlocking or cancelling decides no right, since it only gives up what the owner holds.
locks.notes: §5.11, §3.2 (LockWaitOver: a grant is released only for a refusal, a cancel, the host's restart, an administrator's revoke of its client, or its share's removal), RFC 14 §2.10, RFC 19 §3.8, V23. An NFSv4 lock that conflicts is ErrLocked and the client polls. An adapter that answers ErrBlocked other than as granted calls CancelLock first. A caller who owns the file MUST be admitted without read data, within its share access.

lifecycle.title: Four states, once, in order
table: `New` starts no goroutine and opens nothing.

`Start` serves each [[shard]]'s [[open-state|open state]], reinstalls the [[persistent-open|persistent opens]] the metadata store kept and enters the [[grace-period|grace period]], then opens the shares. Either every step succeeds or the filesystem stays as it was built.
`Drain` refuses new calls with `ErrUnavailable` and waits for the admitted ones. At the deadline it cancels them, though some may already have applied. Nothing is revoked.
`Stop` stops the timers and closes nothing it was handed.
lifecycle.footer: The start order is the store, open state, the [[engine]], [[gc|GC]] and the identity component, then the filesystem, `Serve` and the gateway, then the first pass that opens the configured shares, and the [[adapter|adapters]] last. Stop runs in nearly the reverse order: the GC drains before the filesystem stops, and in a cluster the shards are handed over before `Serve` stops. No option lets the filesystem start with grace already over.
lifecycle.notes: §2.5, V33, V34, V35. Start does not wait for grace to end. Drain is called once every adapter has drained, and in a cluster once Serve has stopped, since an adapter's drain still delivers break acknowledgements, CLOSEs and unlocks. In a cluster the stop order hands over every shard before Serve stops. Decisions: lifecycle methods are not on vfs.Service, so an adapter cannot drain the service under the other protocol; no setting skips grace, which would let a filesystem serve conflicting state before its clients reclaim it. Persistent opens are installed by RFC 14's Recovery.ServeShard before anything is answered (§2.5, Start step 1). The first pass is the node's first reconcile, which opens the shares (§2.5's table, row 5; RFC 23 §2.2). Stop order (§2.5): the adapters, the gateway, (cluster) the handover of every shard this node is primary of, Serve, the GC drain, the filesystem, identity, the engine, open state, the metadata store.

numbers.w1: [[admission]] checks, which no call naming a handle or an open skips
numbers.w2: SMB break deadline. A request held behind a recall is held longer than that.
numbers.w3: causes of [[retry-later|ErrDelay]]. The cause decides how long an [[adapter]] holds a request.
numbers.w4: In a cluster, how far writers through `k` [[primary|primaries]] can pass a hard quota, beyond what concurrent commits add
numbers.w5: interleavings of locks, writes, opens and unlinks that the tests run every night
numbers.w6: memory allocations the service may add to a read or a write. The benchmarks check this target.
numbers.notes: 5 checks: §4.9. 35 s: §3.2, from RFC 14 §5.3. 8 causes: §4.3. (k − 1) × slack: §5.6. 10⁴ interleavings: §8, the integration tier's nightly run of a model of lock, write, open and unlink interleaved under -race. 0 allocations: §8, Benchmarks ('0 allocations on the data path').

tests.title: Tested without a protocol, cheapest first
table: admission, the [[pseudo-filesystem]], quota arithmetic, ID codecs
the filesystem over an in-memory `Content` held to its conformance suite
that every operation's order holds, by checking what each refusal leaves unchanged
every cross-protocol rule, with injected faults, and 10⁴ interleavings every night
two nodes over the network transport on 127.0.0.1, with injected faults
the route envelope, the epoch fence and dedup
the [[adapter|adapters]] over an [[in-memory-service|in-memory filesystem]], then the protocol suites
tests.footer: An architecture test fails if the gateway holds a `*Filesystem`, if `internal/vfs` imports network code, or if any package but `authz` calls the [[chokepoint]].
tests.notes: §8. The conformance suite has one file per area plus crossproto.go and faults.go, driven by Call values of different protocols with no adapter. Fuzz targets: IDs, cursors, handles, names, sequences. The architecture check is seeded with one deliberate violation of each rule. Authorize is the chokepoint's entry point, and authz is its only caller (§4.6). The test doubles are the in-memory store, open state and Content, each held to its conformance suite, and fault wrappers around real components (§8, RFC 29 §4.11). Adapter tests run against an in-memory filesystem, memory.New, itself held to the service's conformance suite (§8, RFC 20 §7).

whom.dev: Adapters import one package, `pkg/vfs`. They keep no share list, check no permission, test no lock and parse no [[handle]]. An adapter translates the request, makes one call and maps the neutral error back to its protocol.
whom.store: The filesystem is their only caller. The metadata store shrinks to plain store operations and stays swappable, and the [[chokepoint]] stays inside it.
whom.ops: Both protocols follow one rule. A revoked grant takes effect on the next call. The service emits every audited access decision and every quota event from one path, so no protocol escapes the audit stream.
whom.notes: Deck's own framing, drawn from §1, §2.1 (decision: the service is a new layer, not a grown metadata store), §3.3 (each decision is audited once), §4.6 and §9.

rules.title: The rules, and what the service never does
items: An [[adapter]] never builds a protocol's behaviour out of weaker service calls.
The [[primary]] orders a conflict check and its I/O so that nothing is granted between them.
A [[callback]] never blocks past its deadline, and handing an audit or quota event to the node never blocks or fails the operation.
A routing refusal never reaches an adapter, and an adapter never parses [[handle|handles]].
The service adds no copy on the data path.
nongoals: encodes a wire format, runs a compound or keeps a reply cache;
evaluates a file permission itself, but asks the [[chokepoint]];
keeps a copy of metadata, [[open-state|open state]] or content beyond the call, except caches keyed by version and the [[pseudo-filesystem]];
persists anything of its own, or imports an adapter;
counts the requests an adapter holds, or refers a client to another [[installation]], a separate set of servers.
rules.notes: Rules: §4.1 (atomic form, or the operation is not supported), §4.8, §3.2 and §3.3 (an event hook MUST NOT block or fail the operation), §4.3, §4.4 (an adapter MUST NOT build, parse or compare handles), §4.5. Non-goals: §1.1, every bullet; the state it may keep is limited to the admission cache (§4.9), the authorisation cache (§4.6) and the pseudo-filesystem, each keyed by the versions it read. Counting held requests is RFC 20 §4.6's and RFC 24's. Numbers of removed V-rows are not reused. §6 lists the invariants, V3 to V42, each with the test that would catch a plausible wrong service. Events: the filesystem builds every access and quota event and hands it to the node's event sink, which queues it (§3.3). Referrals: §1.1, a share is served only by the installation that holds it.

openq.title: Open questions
questions: Should there be a batch call for compounds? Not for now, because only a benchmark on a cluster could show that one is worth it.
pNFS layouts are not in the service. The [[adapter]] answers that they are not supported.
The layers below have three gaps: no field for the token an NFS exclusive create stores, no call that turns an empty file into a symlink, and no way for the service to read quota records.
A [[watch]] can cover a whole subtree. When the subtree's directories sit in several [[shard|shards]], it is not yet decided who registers the watch at each one.
openq.notes: §10 (items 1, 2, 4, 5; item 3, ID widths, is settled by RFC 14 §2.11). Item 4: RFC 7's Attrs has no exclusive-create verifier though RFC 7 §2.10 stores one; RFC 16 declares no read view of quota records but ControlPlane's, which the filesystem must not call. Item 5: a recursive watch must be registered at each directory's primary (RFC 11 §2.2). Item 4 also names no call turning an empty file into a symlink (SMB SET_REPARSE_POINT) (§10 item 4).

quizRefuse.question: In a cluster, build01 writes over NFSv3 to a file alice-pc holds open over SMB with deny-write. What refuses it?
options: The NFS adapter, which checks alice's deny mode before calling the service.
The gateway on the node build01 reached, which checks opens before forwarding.
The filesystem at the file's primary, where the open-state table lives.
why: No [[adapter]] decides a conflict. The NFS adapter turns the write into one call and maps the refusal it gets back to an NFS error.
The [[gateway-node|gateway]] holds no [[open-state|open state]] and decides nothing. It only sends the write on to the file's [[primary]].
Alice's [[deny-mode]] is recorded in the open-state table at the file's [[primary]], and the filesystem there refuses the write with `ErrShareViolation`.
quizRefuse.notes: 'Start here · In plain words' and its six-step example (an anonymous open is checked against the deny modes others hold and refused as a sharing violation); §2 (the gateway decides nothing); §2.2 (the open-state table lives in the filesystem at the file's primary; the gateway holds none of it; the adapter never decides a conflict); §4.6, Deny modes. Had alice's opens been covered by a lease with handle caching, the refusal would come only after that lease was broken (§5.3).

quizRevoked.question: An administrator removes bob's [[share-grant]] while bob-pc still holds handles. What happens to bob-pc's next call?
options: It is refused, because the share grant is checked again on every call.
It succeeds, because bob-pc's access is decided only when it mounts the share.
It succeeds, because a permission result for that file is already cached.
why: [[admission|Admission]] reads bob's grant afresh on each call and the [[chokepoint]] applies it, so with no grant left the call is refused. A [[handle]] grants nothing.
A mount becomes one `Root` call, where a client fails early, but access is not gated there. Every later call is admitted again.
A cached permission result has the version of the share's grant list in its key. Removing the grant changes that version, so the cache cannot answer.
quizRevoked.notes: 'Start here · Scenarios', the RFC's own scenario; §4.6 (the share grant is checked on every call; a cache of authorisation results MUST include the share's grant-list version, which a grant's deletion moves as well as its change; holding a handle grants nothing); §4.9 (Root is where a client fails early, not where it is gated; admission runs on every call). Admission reads the grant (§4.9 step 4, refusing nothing); Authorize applies it as the share ceiling and refuses (§4.6).

quizHandleCaching.question: An open conflicts only with deny modes of opens kept alive by a [[lease]] with handle caching. What does the service do?
options: It refuses the open at once with ErrShareViolation, since those opens exist.
It breaks the lease, answers ErrDelay, and checks the deny modes on the retry.
It breaks the lease and waits for the client to acknowledge before answering.
why: Their client may already have closed those handles, which only the lease keeps open. Refused at once, the open would fail against handles nobody is using.
Some of those opens may be gone after the break. So the service answers `ErrDelay` and checks again, on the retry, against the opens that remain.
No worker waits on a client. The service starts the break and answers `ErrDelay` at once, without waiting for the acknowledgement.
quizHandleCaching.notes: §5.3, 'A sharing violation is decided after handle caching is broken': such a request MUST NOT be refused yet, whatever its protocol; it starts a break, returns ErrDelay, and on its retry re-checks the deny modes against the opens that remain. §3.2, 'No worker waits on a client': the recall starts and ErrDelay returns at once. For an SMB caller the SMB adapter holds and re-drives the request itself (RFC 20 §4.6).

steps: alice-pc's 64 KiB `WRITE` comes through her own open. Her deny mode, which forbids others to write, is recorded in [[open-state|open state]].
Her write passes all six steps, from routing to the [[engine]], which stages it in the journal, and alice-pc gets OK.
build01's NFSv3 write arrives on an [[anonymous-open]]. At step 4 it meets alice's deny mode and is refused as a sharing violation.
The NFS [[adapter]] turns `ErrShareViolation` into an NFS error. One rule, in one place, for both protocols.

route.checked: same checks as a forwarded call
steps: When node A is itself the file's primary, the call goes to node A's own filesystem, still through `Serve`, which runs the same checks as on a forwarded call.
When the primary is node B, the gateway sends the call there with its [[route-envelope]]. `Serve` on node B checks that the call's [[epoch|epochs]] are current, and node B's filesystem decides.
If the reply is lost, the gateway resends the call under the same request ID. `Serve` answers it from its [[dedup-table|dedup table]], so the call is applied only once.

If a new primary has [[takeover|taken over]], the shard's epoch has risen, so the call carries a stale epoch and is refused. The gateway re-routes it to the new primary, and the [[adapter]] never sees the refusal.
build01's write conflicts with alice-pc's SMB [[lease]], so the service starts a lease break.
The service answers `ErrDelay` at once instead of waiting, so no worker is held, and build01 is told to retry.
alice-pc acknowledges the break, and the SMB [[adapter]] passes that on to the service with `AckRecall`.
build01 retries, and this time its write goes ahead.
If alice-pc never answers, the break is forced after 35 s. Her lease loses its caching, but her opens stay.
